articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Sues California Over Voter Rolls
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Sues California Over Voter Rolls
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.
The lawsuit , filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.
"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."
In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."
Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.
"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.
"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.
CBS News has reached out to the secretary of state and the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
articles.content_orig:
Technology giants Nvidia and Cisco have committed millions to President Donald Trump 's White House ballroom renovation project, CNBC confirmed on Thursday.
Nvidia and Apple each pledged $25 million to the project, according to a report from The Washington Post . Those were among the largest donations on the list, which totaled more than $330 million.
"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."
Amazon , Palantir , ServiceNow , Meta Platforms and Microsoft also made contributions in the millions, according to the Post. Microsoft and Meta declined to comment on the report. Cisco confirmed its $5 million donation.
Amazon, Apple, HP Inc. , Micron , Palantir, Salesforce , ServiceNow and Vast Space, which were all listed as major donors in the report, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Post reported that the ballroom donations were sent through a nonprofit trust, and donors received a pledge form for donating to the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom."
Lawmakers and experts have repeatedly called out donations to the project, requesting information on the private donors. Some have also raised concerns over the potential influence these commitments could have on policy decisions or any federal contract awards.
Tech leaders have largely favored Trump's pro-business, light-touch approach to antitrust and regulation, and some companies have secured hundreds of millions in contracts through artificial intelligence infrastructure and defense deals during his second term.
Tech leaders like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have been regulars at state dinners and meetings in Washington, and were central figures at the White House AI luncheon on Sept. 29.
The documents obtained by the Post showed 67 contributions above $10,000 as of late September.

articles.title_orig: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.title_zh: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.content_orig:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple , the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture . As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded , "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
" We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models , it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang , who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman , was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration " dramatically underperformed " and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk 's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google , to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer , with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Thursday as concerns around tech companies overspending on artificial intelligence led investors to rotate out of the trade and seek value elsewhere. Traders also digested U.S. data that pointed to persistent inflation.
The blue-chip index added 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to end at 52,177.69. The S&P 500 gained 0.33% to close at 7,744.06. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed up 0.08% at 26,713.03, rebounding from session lows. At one point, the index was down 1.4% on the day.
Seagate Technology and Western Digital added to their declines this week, along with shares of SK Hynix , which drove a rout in South Korea's Kospi index overnight. Traders were becoming concerned about a potential memory chip glut as South Korea faces increasing competition from China. Tesla CEO Elon Musk discussed the matter in a post on X , saying that "China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028."
Compounding worries in the AI space, sources told CNBC that Anthropic's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter, with some traders concerned the AI giant's top line might not be growing fast enough to justify the lofty gains in chipmakers.
However, other stocks in the AI trade recovered. CoreWeave shares gained almost 6%, reversing course from the prior day's losses. The stock tumbled more than 15% in the previous session as investors grew fearful that the company was borrowing too much for its AI build-out. CoreWeave corporate bond yields also surged . Additionally, Micron Technology rebounded from earlier losses to gain nearly 2%.
"When Treasurys are yielding 5% and that's the highest since the early 2000s, investors are going to start weighing that versus taking a huge bet on on AI," said Alex Shahidi, co-CIO of MAI Capital Management's Evoke. "It's not are you in or out of AI; it's how concentrated you want to be."
The market was supported by gains in areas outside of tech. Shares of retailer Walmart climbed 1.5%, while Nike shares jumped more than 5%.
Investors also reacted to more insights on the inflation front. The September reading on producer prices recorded an increase of 1.3% on the month and 6.3% year over year — the biggest monthly and yearly gains since 2022.
Concerns that the Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy more aggressively before year-end weighed on equities Wednesday after new data showed consumer prices in September rose faster than expected on a year-over-year basis.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
The three major averages finished Thursday's session with gains.
The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to end at 7,744.06, while the Nasdaq Composite gained just 0.08% to 26,713.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to 52,177.69.
Analysts at Barclays say they're seeing signs that a SpaceX - Tesla merger is something that executives are thinking about, analysts with Barclays said Wednesday.
"We believe recent management comments indicate they see key benefits of a combination," analyst Dan Levy wrote to clients in a Wednesday note, though he didn't get into the details.
Vertical integration of production pipelines for two the companies, in addition to the elimination of overhead redundancies, would boost value added, Levy said. He put the Texas-based Terafab data center, which is already structured as a joint venture, at the center of his estimation.
"We see Terafab as a key driver of the potential combination as CEO Elon Musk strongly believes that Terafab will be required to support TSLA/SPCX compute needs," he wrote.
Performance is broadening out within the S&P 500.
More than half of S&P 500 stocks are trading above their 200-day moving averages, an improvement from  less than 40% at the end of September when gains were more concentrated, likely within tech stocks.
Some of the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in more than a month were Walmart ( WMT ), Kroger ( KR ), HCA Healthcare ( HCA ) and United Health Services ( UHS ).
— Nick Wells and Tobias Burns
CoreWeave stock broke into black in Thursday afternoon, trading up 3.5% just as of 2:53 p.m., after being down as much as 9.5% in morning trading.
The uptick proved a Wednesday Deutsche Bank note to be prescient. Analyst Brad Zelnick said that Wednesday's dislocation was "presenting buying opportunity."
"If this is purely about broader AI financing concerns, we'd argue CoreWeave continues to scale rather responsibly," he wrote to clients. "Near-term liquidity is in decent shape."
The stock got hit with a combination blow on Wednesday, with higher-than-expected inflation data initially pushing up bond yields, industrial titans fretting about the stock online, and some warnings from analysts about its sector.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is lower for an eighth straight trading day, its first eight-day slide since September 2015; it fell for nine sessions in May 2006. The ETF has fallen more than 15% over that stretch. The fund was last down around 2%.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is also down an eighth straight day, making it the longest slide since May 2006 when it fell for nine straight sessions.
— Sarah Min and Nick Wells
More than half of S&P 500 constituents are trading above their 200-day moving averages, a notable improvement from late September when that figure was around 40%.
The shift suggests that participation in the market's advance is broadening beyond recent high flyers of the AI trade. The 200-day moving average is a widely watched indicator of a stocks' long-term trend and a shift above that level can show improving momentum.
Among the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in a month are Walmart , Kroger , HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services .
Wall Street firm Baird upgraded Bank of America to outperform from neutral Thursday, while maintaining its $62 price target, implying a 21% upside from its Wednesday close of $51.
The higher rerating on the bank comes despite it reporting a soft quarter before the open Thursday.
Bank of America delivered an earnings per share miss and weak noninterest income along with higher expenses on Wednesday, sending shares lower.
Baird called the sell-off "overdone" and sees the stock's weakness as a buying opportunity. That stems from the firm's view that the bank's 2027 net interest income outlook is an "incremental positive" coupled with the stock's attractive valuation.
Gil Luria, analyst at DA Davidson, said Anthropic's revenue for the third quarter was "not what anyone wanted to see."
Sources told CNBC that the AI giant's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter , up from its second-quarter revenue of $11.6 billion. But, that growth in the third quarter was slower than its rise in the previous one, as first-quarter revenue for the company was just $4.7 billion.
Luria said, though, that there was good news as the Financial Times reported that Antrhopic had positive cash flow in the third quarter, pushing back on the narrative that the AI labs can't get to profitability. But he added that investors shouldn't be looking at a single company to judge the performance of the sector, and rather focus on corporate and consumer spending on the technology.
"We expect the overall market for AI spend to continue on a steep path as it diversifies away from Anthropic and OpenAI," he wrote in a Thursday note. "These two will see their market get cut from providing all-encompassing AI services to only providing frontier tokens for mission critical cost-insensitive applications… This overall demand should support more AI compute demand and more data center construction, even if it doesn't meet the most outlandish extrapolations."

articles.title_orig: Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led coalition forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden
articles.title_zh: Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led coalition forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden
articles.content_orig:
Witnesses report at least six explosions near palace used by Yemen's internationally recognized government
At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by Yemen ’s internationally recognized government in the port city of Aden, witnesses said.
An official told the Associated Press that at least two people were killed, and Iran -backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility. Government military sources in Yemen told Agence-France Press (AFP) that at least four people were killed and 10 wounded.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Yemeni prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”.
It was a rare attack on the palace area, as fighting has escalated between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition on the latest front in the Iran war. The explosions caused panic among residents, who fled the area.
At least two people were killed and six wounded, said the official, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The government said the Houthis attacked with missiles and drones, the Aden-based Saba news agency reported.
A security official told the AP that at least two explosions were on top of the hill near Al-Maashiq palace, and two others were near the security gate.
AFP also reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity on Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command center for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command center was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
There was no immediate confirmation of the report that the prime minister was in the presidential palace at the time of Houthi attack. Many of Yemen’s government leaders are living in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official told the AP.
The Houthis said they attacked a military operations headquarters with the “Saudi enemy”, part of their strategy of attacking Saudi targets that has included a series of attacks on airports and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom.
The escalation has complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia , one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted.
Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport.
The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase.
Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said the headquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks , and reported damage to the building.
Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.

articles.title_orig: Scientists Uncover D. Rex: Gigantic New 'King' Fungus From China Traces Its Roots to 65 Million Years
articles.title_zh: Scientists Uncover D. Rex: Gigantic New 'King' Fungus From China Traces Its Roots to 65 Million Years
articles.content_orig:
Yunnan Province in China is famous for its mushrooms and fungi, but somehow, scientists have only just come across a new species that has rightly earned the name 'king'.
Named Dianjunus rex (or D. rex for short), its gigantic, club-like fruiting bodies can grow up to 50 centimeters tall, which is about one and a half feet, or the height of a traffic cone.
But its impressive size is not the only exciting thing about this fungus. Its genes also contain clues about a major moment in the history of life on Earth.
Mycologist Indunil Senanayake of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and her colleagues describe the new species in a paper published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology .
D. rex is the only known member of its family, Dianjunaceae .
"This remarkable species… provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms," says Senanayake.
"The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests."
D. rex's fruiting bodies were discovered in the forests of Yunnan Province. (Song et al., Frontiers in Fungal Biology , 2026)
The researchers found the Dianjunaceae family split off from its closest known relatives about 65 million years ago, by comparing its DNA to hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary history is well-known.
"This timing raises an intriguing possibility," says Senanayake.
The family emerged just 1 million years after the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered a mass extinction event.
The dramatic changes to Earth's climate that resulted from the asteroid wiped out three-quarters of plant and animal species on Earth, including, famously, all non-avian dinosaurs .
"After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material," Senanayake says .
"For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities."
This isn't the first time scientists have proposed that the dinosaur-killing asteroid led to a worldwide fungal 'boom' . Fossils found in North Dakota, Colorado, and New Zealand show that massive spikes in fungal activity followed in the wake of this mass extinction.
Fungi typically prefer cooler temperatures and acidic environments. The cooler and darker conditions that arise when geological calamities shade our skies – as Chicxulub did – could have easily set the scene for an era dominated by fungi.
Close examination of D. rex under a microscope reveals its identifying features, including its asci and spore-producing structures (h-p). (Song et al., Frontiers in Fungal Biology , 2026)
D. rex is related to fungi like morels, truffles, and cordyceps , in the phylum Ascomycota . Like all fungi, Ascomycetes live as mycelium, below the ground or inside the substrates (wood, poop, your toenails, etc.) upon which they feed.
D. rex is often found at the base of oak trees, including the Chinese cork oak ( Quercus variabilis ) in the forests of the Yunnan Province in south-western China. The specimens on record so far were growing on the decaying roots or stumps of these trees.
When it comes time to reproduce, D. rex sends out its gigantic white fruiting bodies, which are called stromata. These serve the same purpose as mushrooms do for other fungi, broadcasting spores into the air so more D. rex may flourish on the forest floor.
But it's unclear why D. rex 's stromata are quite so gargantuan – the largest of any Ascomycete on record. Some specimens the researchers collected weighed a whopping 2.2 kilograms.
"A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests," Senanayake proposes .
"However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs."
The research has been published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology .

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave's slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave's slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave 's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive .
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft , Meta , IBM and Caterpillar , Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle 's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

articles.title_orig: The largest croquet club in the world is on the Northern Neck. It's hosting the North American championships this weekend
articles.title_zh: The largest croquet club in the world is on the Northern Neck. It's hosting the North American championships this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Contrary to what you might think, it’s not all in the wrist when you’re playing golf croquet.
“Actually, the wrist is something that interferes with hitting a straight shot,” said George Enoch. “You kind of swing from your shoulders. You obviously have to use your wrist because you've got to rotate the ball when you hit it. But if you have too much wrist action, you're liable to hit the ball off-center. And if you hit it off-center, it's not going to go where you want it to.”
Enoch, 87, is practicing his shots on one of the 24 laser-leveled, Bermuda grass courts at the Chesapeake Bay Croquet Club, which sits roughly 500 yards from one of the many inlets into the Chesapeake Bay just outside of Hartfield. He’s here hoping to win a trophy at the North American Open Golf Croquet Championship taking place this weekend.
“I live up in Alexandria,” said Enoch, who’s been playing for 40 years and has traveled to other states to compete. “It's a two-and-a-half-hour drive away, and I can come down here and play competitively without a whole lot of inconvenience.”
The event and location is part of Macey White’s croquet empire, something he started building more than a decade ago. The club is celebrating its 10th anniversary.
“I started playing croquet when I was 53 years old,” said White, now 66. “And at 53 you can't be internationally competitive in a lot of things. Basketball is out. Football is out. But croquet, you can learn the game at 53, make your national team – which I did. It's a low-impact sport.”
He fell in love with the sport and decided to create his own club in his own back yard that once held dozens of peach trees when it belonged to his grandfather. White’s grandfather’s house — which he now lives in — sits within walking distance to the courts.
“I spent the winter pulling all the trees, moving topsoil, leveling the subsoil and putting the topsoil back,” he said. “Sometime in August, we had courts we could play on. And in October, we ran a tournament. We started this club with two members and eight courts. We fell in love with running tournaments and having people come from other places.”
Now White has 24 courts and a clubhouse that was once a barn.
“We built this into the largest facility in the world,” he said. “We were twice the size of the next biggest club in the world, which was the National Croquet Center in West Palm Beach. Since then, they've tried to catch us, so they have 15 courts now. But we're still the largest with 24, probably always will be.”
The style of croquet that’s being played this weekend is known as Golf Croquet. It’s one of the forms of competitive croquet that’s played in the United States, said White, who has been national champion nine times in a form known as nine-wicket.
“A lot of people play croquet in their backyard,” he said. “When you play that by the actual rules and not just try to send your sister's ball into the bushes, it's a very competitive and complex game. And it is still played on long grass.”
The other forms of the sport are played on short grass.
“The nine-wicket is purely American and on short grass, (and) six-wicket is purely American. They're very similar,” White said. “A similar game internationally is called association croquet. It's the most widely played form of croquet in the world. The U.S. has won the world championship in golf croquet three (tournaments) running.”
The tournament at the club draws people from all over the country and the world, especially when they held the World Championships in 2024.
Silvia Short and her husband Peter Dreyer recently moved from South Africa to North Carolina. She said they’re still learning how to play golf croquet.
“This is already our second tournament, and we've only been here a month,” said Short, who’s been playing since 2009. “We weren't taught golf croquet. We were taught association tournament croquet, which is, I think, more the original form of the game. It's like snooker. You make as many hoops as you can and try to win the game.”
Short, 70, who represented South Africa in the Women's World Championships in England in 2023, said her and Dreyer are predicted to win a trophy on Sunday.
“Our seedings came in quite high, which is quite surprising. Peter is first in his block, and I'm second in my block, so the challenge is ours,” she said.
John Welch and his wife came down from Plymouth, Massachusetts to compete. The 77-year-old has been playing for 11 years after having to give up playing basketball due to health issues.
“We're playing as a team and we just lost a tough 7-6 match, so it could be a long ride home. Nobody talking to each other,” he said, with a laugh. “I got into croquet and it fulfills my competitive instincts. In my own mind, I'm very well-ranked.”
Enoch likes that the sport has a lot to offer for both body and mind.
“It has a physical component to it. You've got to be able to physically execute the shots,” he said. “It has an intellectual component because you've got to figure out the strategy, which shots to hit and how to hit them. And (at) my age, it gives me something to be competitive about.”
Despite the age range of the players on the courts in Chesapeake Bay, White said the game is not just for older people. In fact American Blake Fields won the Golf Croquet World Championship in 2024 at age 18.
“Interestingly, the age range is really wide. It's a game that you can play your entire life,” he said. “There are some who are 13, 14, 15-years-old who are winning tournaments, and there's guys in their 80s that are winning tournaments.”
Every Sunday, the club offers free lessons from pros, and games for anyone.
Wednesday’s tournament started with round robins and gave the players a chance to warm up, said White. Then starting Friday afternoon, the playoffs will start.
“They'll take two and a half days to finish, so sometime Sunday afternoon we'll have the finals for both the doubles and the singles,” White said.

articles.title_orig: Shipwreck believed to be the world's oldest discovered off the coast of Turkey
articles.title_zh: Shipwreck believed to be the world's oldest discovered off the coast of Turkey
articles.content_orig:
Archaeologists estimated that the cargo ship sank 4,400 to 4,700 years ago.
Archaeologists announced they have discovered the remains of the world's oldest shipwreck, a wooden cargo vessel they estimated sank off the coast of Turkey nearly 5,000 years ago.
Hakan Öniz, who led the underwater excavation, said the shipwreck dates back to when the Great Pyramid of Giza was being constructed.
Among the artifacts recovered from the ship, estimated to be around 30 feet long, were ceramic storage pots and clay containers that may have been used to transport olive oil and wine, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, the Turkish minister of culture and tourism, said in a social media post on Wednesday.
Ersoy said one of the amphoras, or containers, recovered featured nine different markings and two holes in its body and may have been used to churn cheese or butter.
Ersoy said the discovery could shed light on the history of the maritime trade along the Anatolian coasts.
In an interview with the BBC , Öniz, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition, estimated the ship sank near Kekova Island, off the southern coast of Turkey, 4,400 to 4,700 years ago during the early Bronze Age.
"We are the first humans who touched these objects after about 5,000 years," Öniz, head of the Mediterranean Underway Cultural Heritage Division at Akdeniz University in Antalya, Turkey, told the BBC.
He said the wreck was discovered in about 100 feet of water.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," Öniz told the BBC.

articles.title_orig: DRAM Giants Get Rich as China Builds a Threat - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: DRAM Giants Get Rich as China Builds a Threat - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Micron, Samsung and SK hynix are posting some of the most spectacular profits in semiconductor history, but a Chinese competitor is quietly building the capacity to dismantle the very conditions making those profits possible.
Micron Technology ( MU ), Samsung Electronics and SK hynix ( SKHY ) are making a fortune from the global memory shortage, and their customers are paying for it. Artificial intelligence infrastructure investment has driven extraordinary demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), server DRAM and other advanced memory products, while constrained supplies have sent prices soaring. Wall Street is celebrating the resulting profits, but investors should be asking whether the industry’s three dominant manufacturers are becoming dangerously comfortable with a market in which scarcity generates exceptional returns.
Micron’s financial results expose just how lucrative the memory shortage has become. In fiscal 2026, the company generated $133.19 billion in revenue, up 256% from $37.38 billion in fiscal 2025. Its GAAP gross margin more than doubled from 39.8% to 80.7%, while net income surged from $8.54 billion to $84.97 billion. Most revealing, Micron reported that DRAM average selling prices increased approximately 180% year over year, compared with bit shipment growth in only the mid-20% range. The enormous expansion in profitability was driven primarily by customers paying dramatically higher prices, not a comparable increase in memory production.
The three manufacturers have continued spending heavily on new technology and production facilities, but their investments have increasingly favored the most profitable products, particularly HBM and advanced server DRAM. The strategy is rational from the perspective of maximizing shareholder returns, but its consequences extend beyond the companies’ income statements. Conventional DRAM supply remains constrained, customers face sharply higher prices, and the manufacturers benefit from a market in which additional production has not kept pace with demand.
Meanwhile, China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is pursuing a strategy that could eventually undermine the very scarcity that has made the established manufacturers so profitable. Despite restrictions on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment and its inability to acquire EUV lithography systems, CXMT has continued developing more sophisticated DRAM technologies while preparing a substantial expansion in manufacturing capacity.
The irony is difficult to ignore. Micron, Samsung and SK hynix are collecting the rewards of today’s shortage while China is investing to make sure those rewards do not last forever.
The memory industry has a long history of manufacturers expanding production too aggressively, creating oversupply and watching prices collapse. Following the severe downturn in 2022 and 2023, Micron, Samsung and SK hynix reduced production or moderated certain investments to restore profitability. That response was understandable, but the industry’s subsequent emphasis on protecting margins has become particularly lucrative as AI infrastructure spending accelerates.
HBM has become central to this strategy. Used alongside advanced AI processors, HBM commands premium prices and requires sophisticated manufacturing and packaging. The established manufacturers have increasingly directed capital and production resources toward these products, seeking the highest possible returns from an industry experiencing unprecedented demand.
There is nothing inherently improper about maximizing profits. The problem is that the three manufacturers may be confusing their ability to profit from scarcity with an enduring competitive advantage. The more attractive DRAM prices become, the stronger the incentive for China to develop its own alternative suppliers.
CXMT is responding to that incentive with manufacturing investment. Unlike the established producers, whose capital allocation decisions are closely tied to near-term financial returns, CXMT operates within China’s broader objective of reducing dependence on foreign semiconductor suppliers. Its investments therefore reflect strategic considerations that extend beyond the profitability of any individual memory cycle.
According to Table 1, CXMT’s estimated installed DRAM wafer capacity is projected to increase from 300,000 wafers per month at the end of 2025 to 550,000 by the end of 2028, representing growth of 83.3%. The expansion includes additional capacity at Hefei and Beijing, along with a new manufacturing contribution from Shanghai beginning in 2027.
Table 1. CXMT DRAM Manufacturing Capacity by Location, 2025–2028E
Thousands of wafers per month, year-end
The projected expansion is significant because additional wafer capacity is only one component of CXMT’s potential growth in memory production. Improvements in DRAM cell density can increase the number of memory bits manufactured on each wafer, while higher yields can increase the number of usable chips. If CXMT successfully combines capacity expansion with technological improvements, its growth in marketable memory output could exceed the growth in installed wafer capacity.
These forecasts are not guarantees. Equipment restrictions, process complexity, manufacturing yields and construction schedules could delay expansion. Nevertheless, the projections demonstrate the scale of China’s ambitions in DRAM manufacturing. While the established manufacturers enjoy extraordinary margins, CXMT is developing the manufacturing infrastructure needed to become a more consequential competitor.
The strategic danger is that the current shortage is making China’s investment case more compelling. High DRAM prices increase the economic value of domestic production, while dependence on foreign suppliers reinforces Beijing’s determination to develop alternatives. The established manufacturers may be maximizing today’s profits while strengthening the incentives for their future competition.
The established DRAM manufacturers could dismiss CXMT as a producer of older, less sophisticated memory products. That argument is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.
CXMT has advanced beyond DDR4 into DDR5 and LPDDR5X, while pursuing next-generation mobile memory, advanced server DRAM and HBM technologies. These developments matter because the company’s ambitions now extend into product categories that have historically supported the established manufacturers’ technological advantages and premium pricing.
Industry estimates of CXMT’s 2026 product mix indicate approximately 25% DDR4, 25% DDR5 and 50% LPDDR5X. Although these are estimates rather than confirmed shipment shares, they suggest that CXMT is no longer concentrating primarily on legacy memory. The company is positioning itself to compete in increasingly sophisticated applications.
Its proposed 4F² DRAM architecture represents a potentially important technological development. Conventional DRAM memory cells commonly use a 6F² design, where F represents the minimum feature dimension. At the same feature dimension, reducing the memory-cell footprint from 6F² to 4F² decreases theoretical cell area by one-third, potentially increasing memory-cell density by 50%.
The distinction between theoretical density and commercial manufacturing performance is important. CXMT has not demonstrated that its proposed 4F² architecture can achieve competitive production yields, reliability or costs at scale. Samsung and SK hynix are also developing advanced memory-cell architectures, and the established manufacturers retain considerable manufacturing advantages.
Nevertheless, CXMT is attacking the technological problem from a different direction. Rather than relying entirely on smaller lithographic dimensions, it is pursuing architectural changes that can increase memory capacity within a given chip area. That approach is especially significant for a manufacturer operating without access to EUV lithography.

articles.title_orig: China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox.
By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension.
As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.
The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials.
That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.
That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security.
China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench.
Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power.
Rare earths may not define the South China Sea today, but they could help reshape how its strategic value is imagined tomorrow.

articles.title_orig: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
articles.title_zh: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
articles.content_orig:
One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don’t react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain.
“Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min’s team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect.
Min’s lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.”
Many animal studies have tied microplastic toxicity to oxidative stress, which is caused by ROS. So the team wondered if the boundary between water and plastic might do something similar. “We got inspired by that field,” Min said.
In the first test, the team stirred polystyrene powder into water containing methyl orange, a yellow dye that ROS break apart. Over 10 days, the solution faded almost to colorless, losing nearly 90 percent of the dye. In ethanol or other solvents, the dye stayed intact. Min and his colleagues concluded that whatever chemistry polystyrene was undergoing needed water to happen. So they ran more tests.
First was electron spin resonance, a technique that directly detects radicals—atoms or molecules with an unpaired electron that makes them particularly reactive. The polystyrene powder and water mixture contained hydroxyl radicals, a highly reactive ROS.
Next, the team used a fluorescent sensor that lights up only when it reacts with hydroxyl radicals. “You don’t see it, but once it reacts with local ROS, it turns into a bright color,” Min said. Under a microscope, the glow concentrated on the surfaces of the plastic particles and kept building over time.
The effect was not unique to polystyrene either. Scientists tested six common plastics—polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, PVC, PET, and acrylic—and all of them generated radicals. The most water-repellent plastics, polyethylene and polypropylene, were the most active, while PET and acrylic, which contain chemical groups that attract water, were the least.
“The simplest answer is the most water-repellent ones change the water structure the most,” Min said. In ordinary, or bulk, water, each molecule is held in a network of hydrogen bonds with its neighbors. But a few layers of water molecules pressed against a water-repellent surface lose some of those partners. “Their structure is no longer the regular water structure. They are perturbed, and their energy is also significantly increased,” Min said.
Water always contains a small number of hydroxide ions, and turning one into a hydroxyl radical requires stripping away an electron. In bulk water, that costs a lot of energy. But simulations run by the group showed that, at a polyethylene surface, hydroxide ions short on hydrogen bonds needed far less energy to form radicals. On top of that, the plastic surfaces build up a negative electric charge in water, which further lowered the energy cost.
But Min’s team still had doubts to address before making any conclusive claims.
Min’s earlier work on microdroplet chemistry has drawn a lot of criticism, with some researchers arguing that the reported reactive chemicals come from contamination or measurement artifacts.
To avoid similar objections, Min and his colleagues used several independent detection methods. They also added a detergent-like surfactant that coats the plastic and disrupts the water layer at its surface. They found that the more surfactant they added, the weaker the plastic’s electric charge became and the fewer radicals it produced. “We only change one parameter while keeping all the rest [the same],” Min said. “We’re using exactly the same plastics, the same water, the same everything.”
Impurities, Min explained, are typically stable molecules with no reason to spontaneously generate radicals. He is careful not to overstate it, though. “To be absolutely clear, we cannot 100 percent rule out the involvement of impurities,” he said. “But our controls and our theoretical computation studies highly suggest that this is intrinsic to the microplastic-water interface.”
Finally, the team tested if this interface chemistry matters for biological molecules. And it most likely does.
Proteins and DNA can gather on plastic surfaces, and lysozyme, a common test protein, also began clumping into aggregates there. Adding caffeine, which mops up radicals, largely stopped the clumping, pointing to the radicals as the cause.
Mouse red blood cells that touched polystyrene particles broke into fragments, and the damage from each type of plastic tracked how many radicals it produced. The effect also persisted in blood serum.
Min stressed, though, that this indicates that microplastics make people sick by generating ROS. While animal studies often point to ROS as possible roots of oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, ROS can be produced in many ways, including through basic metabolic activity.
Min admitted comparing the magnitude of this effect to the impact of ROS our own cells make is rather tricky.
“If you are really at the interface, you could be significantly affected by this effect, whereas if you are just a few microns away, you don’t feel it anymore,” Min said. Exposure is another unknown here. Min also emphasized that no one can yet say how many microplastics an average person takes in each year from food, water, and air.
The plastics in the study were mostly fresh, lab-bought powders, unlike weathered particles we encounter in the environment. In the team’s tests, older particles with more oxidized surfaces produced somewhat weaker signals. “This aging process is very heterogeneous,” Min said. “Some microplastic particles were made 50 years ago, some were made five days ago.” Finally, there is the question of size.
Microplastics are usually defined as particles smaller than five millimeters, while the minimum cutoff varies between 100 and 1,000 nanometers. Min’s team did not test how variation in microplastic particle size affects water-interface chemistry, but the researchers suspect it might play a role. The same mass of plastic broken into nanoparticles has far more surface area, which might make the effect larger. “This may be another reason for nanoplastics to be more dangerous,” Min said.
The researchers argue that if water-repellent surfaces drive the water interface chemistry, plastics could be designed to be less water-repellent, either by changing their molecular structure or including additives. First, though, the team wants to focus on the question their study left open. “We definitely want to see how much this effect is directly contributing to disease or biological problems in animals and humans,” Min said.

articles.title_orig: China bought half of Brazil’s oil exports as Iran war drove sales to record
articles.title_zh: China bought half of Brazil’s oil exports as Iran war drove sales to record
articles.content_orig:
Crude makes up a quarter of Brazilian shipments to Chinese buyers, but growth has slowed since Gulf tankers started sailing again
Trade between Brazil and China reached a record US$143 billion in the first nine months of the year, driven by Brazilian oil sales that surged after the war on Iran disrupted Gulf supply, according to a report by the Brazil-China Business Council.
Crude oil accounted for most of the gain, with sales to China jumping 49 per cent to a record US$21.8 billion as shipments rose 27 per cent by volume and prices climbed 16.8 per cent. China took half of all the crude Brazil exported, nearly seven times the share of India, the next-largest buyer.

articles.title_orig: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
articles.title_zh: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
articles.content_orig:
Tesla is planning to show off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car.
The event will be livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. It's expected to begin at 7:55 local time (8:55 ET).
Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, used a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.
The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.
Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets.
Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."
Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either.
Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests.
"I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court over a separate matter earlier this year related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure.
Others have kept their reservations.
Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000.
O'Connor wrote in a message that he plans to attend Thursday's event and is "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making."
According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues.
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: MAGA donor hits Guilfoyle, attorneys with defamation lawsuit
articles.title_zh: MAGA donor hits Guilfoyle, attorneys with defamation lawsuit
articles.content_orig:
Eric Deters, the Republican donor who accused Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, has filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle and her legal team.
Guilfoyle was pushed out of her ambassadorship to Greece earlier this week, announcing her resignation Tuesday. Guilfoyle's team publicly disputed the authenticity of text messages Deters shared with multiple news outlets, including CBS News.
Deters filed the lawsuit in Kentucky state court on Thursday.
Deters said Guilfoyle's legal team issued a statement to the Wall Street Journal claiming Deters owed Guilfoyle money and did not fulfill his obligations. The Journal published part of her attorney's statement, that Guilfoyle "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events," which Deters denies.
"Kim Guilfoyle and her lawyers claimed my allegations were false and they would defend the allegations vigorously," Deters wrote in a statement accompanying his lawsuit. "Now they can in Kentucky."
CBS News has reached out to the attorneys named in the lawsuit — Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz — for comment.

articles.title_orig: World losing ground in ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
articles.title_zh: World losing ground in ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.
“ Biodiversity underpins life on Earth ,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people .”
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline , the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“ This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended ,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.
Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul wasted no time in bringing up President Donald Trump as she attacked her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman in their only debate.
But it took more than 40 minutes for Blakeman to mention the bogeyman who helped him cruise to re-election last year as Nassau County executive: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Chapin Fay, a spokesperson for Strong and Safe New York, a super PAC backing Blakeman, said it comes down to popularity.
“Mayor Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians on planet Earth. Kathy Hochul, who is notably not, is trying to tie herself to the mayor,” Fay said. “Why would Blakeman do the job for her?”
A Siena University poll released last month found 46% of likely voters around the state viewed Mamdani favorably, compared to 48% for Hochul, 35% for Blakeman and 34% for Trump.
During an hourlong debate hosted by Spectrum News and broadcast around the state, Hochul and Blakeman clashed over data centers, immigration policy and state spending.
The democratic socialist mayor’s name came up fewer than 10 times. Trump, by contrast, was mentioned more than 50 times.
“I did not wrap myself in the shroud of Donald Trump the way you did,” Hochul charged Blakeman at one point.
“No, you wrapped it in Zohran Mamdani,” Blakeman replied.
“Who Donald Trump actually thinks is a great mayor,” Hochul retorted, a reference to multiple positive joint appearances between the president and the mayor.
Blakeman said he didn’t bring up Mamdani earlier because he wasn’t asked about him.
The county executive went on to call Mamdani an antisemite, but complimented him for keeping Jessica Tisch in place as NYPD commissioner. Mamdani, who has been fiercely critical of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, said Blakeman’s attacks were racist. The mayor has appeared with Jewish leaders and repeatedly denounced antisemitic vandalism and other crimes.
Hochul, a moderate, rejected Blakeman’s characterization and called Mamdani “a partner.” She said the two are planning to campaign together.
“I invited him to watch a Buffalo Bills game with me like we did last year,” said Hochul, an Erie County native. “Given that the Bills are looking so good these days, I think he'd enjoy the experience.”

articles.title_orig: Opinion | I moved up my flu shot appointment. You should, too.
articles.title_zh: Opinion | I moved up my flu shot appointment. You should, too.
articles.content_orig:
by Abigail Taylor | News Channel 3
KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Flu season appears to be arriving earlier than usual in parts of the United States, and Kalamazoo County health officials are urging residents to get vaccinated now even though local flu numbers are not showing an unusual spike.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported the highest rates of early-season influenza on the West Coast and has been tracking cases since late August.
In Kalamazoo County, health officials are “not seeing anything striking in terms of numbers."
An important note: influenza data is counted only through official in-office care or hospital visits.
According to Matt Johnson, a spokesperson for the Kalamazoo County Health & Community Services Department, officials look at trends elsewhere when making recommendations locally.
“We look at some trends in other places, the West Coast or Australia, on if we think the flu season might be coming early or later," Johnson told News Channel 3.
Health officials also say early cases help fine-tune the active pharmaceutical ingredients of any given season’s vaccine.
Regardless of which strain ends up circulating most around West Michigan, according to Johnson, the vaccine being offered is worth getting.
“To have your immune system trained against fighting the flu, even if it’s a, you know, influenza A, influenza B, versus having no flu shot,” Johnson said.
Everyone 6 months and older should get an annual flu vaccine, especially those at higher risk of health complications, including young children, pregnant women, adults with chronic health conditions, and adults over age 50, according to the Kalamazoo County Health & Community Services Department.
Health officials say, if someone gets vaccinated and still catches the flu, the vaccine can also make symptoms milder and shorten the length of illness.
They also said vaccination can help prevent spreading the flu to others, including people at higher risk of serious illness.
“Getting your flu shot is one of the simplest steps you can take to protect yourself, your loved ones, and your community,” Kalamazoo County Health Officer Deb Lenz said. “By getting vaccinated each year, you help reduce the spread of flu and keep our community healthier.”
Kalamazoo County's Health & Community Services Department also reminds of the sometimes underestimated steps to reduce the spread of flu and other germs, such as:
Influenza is a seasonal respiratory illness that impacts communities worldwide.
Health officials said flu season typically starts in October and can last as late as May. They add that the flu shot takes about two weeks to provide full protection.
For that reason, the Kalamazoo County Health & Community Services Department recommends planning to get vaccinated at least a couple weeks before your first holiday gathering.
Flu vaccines are offered with no appointment needed at the Kalamazoo County Health & Community Services Department, Monday through Friday.
Available times include: Monday through Thursday from 8 a.m. to noon and 1-4 p.m., as well as every Friday between 8 a.m. and noon.
The department also has planned community clinics coming up, including:
According to Johnson, Kalamazoo County officials are seeing the biggest dip in vaccinations among people in their 20s to 40s.
He said many people don't realize the options available, like free walk-up options through many stores and pharmacies.
Those in need of a flu vaccine are asked to bring their ID and an insurance card if available, but Johnson said the department will not turn any Kalamazoo County residents away from getting their vaccine.
