articles.title_orig: HIMA China Innovation Center debuts at German Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai
articles.title_zh: HIMA China Innovation Center debuts at German Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai
articles.content_orig:
The opening of the HIMA China Innovation Center is celebrated by (left to right) Zena Zhou, GM of HIMA China), Daisy Zhu, deputy executive director of the German Chamber of Commerce in China—East China, and Jörg de la Motte, CEO of HIMA Group.
While cohosting Operational Excellence (OpEx) Day with the German Chamber of Commerce in China (GCC) , HIMA Group introduced Sept. 15 its new HIMA China Innovation Center (CIC). The event highlighted HIMA’s localization journey in China and provided deeper insights into functional safety and OT security, while showcasing how its solutions protect people, assets and the environment.
HIMA Group reports it brought its functional safety expertise to the Chinese market in 2002, laying the foundation for partnership with local players. It established its wholly owned subsidiary HIMA (Shanghai) Industrial Automation Co. in 2016, marking a landmark shift from market representation to fully localized operation, technical service and project delivery. This year marks the 10-year anniversary of HIMA China’s operations, reflecting a decade of deep market trust and sustained growth.
To continue HIMA’s commitment to excellence, the new CIC will focus on developing safety applications and digital solutions tailored to the evolving needs of China’s industries, fulfill local requirements, and contribute to HIMA’s global innovation roadmap. The center will operate under a dedicated HIMA China Innovation Board, ensuring strong governance and alignment with the group’s strategic objectives. A streamlined, group-wide innovation process will leverage best practices across the organization, enabling rapid ideation, validation and implementation of projects.
In addition, CIC will serve as a collaborative platform, engaging customers, institutes, technology partners and industry experts to co-create future technological solutions. Key focus areas include digitalization, industrial cybersecurity and intelligent systems that support China’s push toward high-quality manufacturing and operational excellence. Ultimately, it serves to foster a win-win ecosystem through stronger connections and shared industry intelligence.
“Launching the HIMA China Innovation Center is an important next step in HIMA China’s development,” says Jörg de la Motte, CEO of HIMA Group. “We’re combining HIMA's unique expertise with the local innovation capabilities of our team in China to develop solutions that create value for customers in China and beyond.”
HIMA reports the CIC has a structured roadmap for safety applications and digital solutions, paving the way for continued expansion of its safety business in China. Since its inception, this initiative achieved several important milestones. For example, a key achievement was the official launch of HIMA’s HMI local version software, which not only delivers traditional HMI functionalities, but also integrates digital features to support smarter, more efficient operations.
“The China Innovation Center launch is a major milestone for our 24 years journey in China,” adds Zhou Yao (Zena), GM of HIMA China. “This is an open platform that brings together HIMA’s global safety expertise with local customers, institutes, EPCs, OEMs and partners. Our vision is clear—innovation without borders. To deliver it, our core aims are: build a strong local system, solve real safety challenges, develop local talent, and export Chinese innovations globally. In practice, we’re prioritizing digitalization, cybersecurity and intelligent systems, by working closely with local partners, we create solutions that meet China’s needs while also delivering value to industries worldwide.”

articles.title_orig: Yemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure
articles.title_zh: Yemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthis have hit the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in the port city of Aden with multiple missiles.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.
The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.
Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.
The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.
“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.
The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.
Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.
Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.
The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.
Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.
On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

articles.title_orig: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
articles.title_zh: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
articles.content_orig:
International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
A fter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.
Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.
The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.
“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”
The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.
“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.
The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.
Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.
Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.
Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.
The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.
“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.
after newsletter promotion
“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.
Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.
To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.
Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.
The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.
Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

Featuring a book by Kate Wetherhead and music and lyrics by Mark Sonnenblick, who won a Grammy and Academy Award for KPop Demon Hunters , the musical finds Kristy, Mary Anne, Claudia, and Stacey now 25 years old, as they return to Stoneybrook for an overdue reunion. Launched by Scholastic in 1986, The Baby-sitters Club by Ann M. Martin is one of the most successful children’s book series in publishing history, with more than 200 million books in print worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
articles.title_zh: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
articles.content_orig:
Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".
He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.
Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.
The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

articles.title_orig: The world's coral reefs are running out of time
articles.title_zh: The world's coral reefs are running out of time
articles.content_orig:
This summer’s record-breaking wildfires have made the consequences of climate change impossible to ignore. As forests burn, the damage is visible. Smoke, blackened trees and an advancing fireline. But the real test often comes afterwards: can the forest recover, re-establish and provide the services that communities rely upon before the next fire arrives?
The world's coral reefs have faced a similar problem for decades, only largely out of sight.
For years, the fate of coral reefs has been presented as a countdown. Warm the planet enough, the argument goes, and reefs will disappear by 2050. That makes for a compelling warning, but it obscures a more complicated, and more consequential, truth. Coral reefs are not simply dying. They have shown the capacity to recover between disturbances, rebuilding coral cover when conditions allow. The concern is that time for this recovery is being diminished.
That is the central message of the Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025 , published on August 31st 2026, by the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN). Over the past four decades coral cover has declined from 30.2% (1980-2009) to 27.3% (2020-2024), a relative decline of around 9.5%, primarily driven by climate change-induced heat stress.
Since 1998, four major global bleaching events have resulted in global losses of coral cover. Bleaching is not a new phenomenon, but climate change has turned episodic shocks into more frequent, severe and recurring pressure. The interval between global bleaching events has fallen from roughly a decade to four to six years, and recovery is therefore becoming a race against time. Yet reefs can still recover. Between 2017 and 2019, after the third global bleaching event, global hard-coral cover increased by 6%, demonstrating the capacity for partial recovery when disturbance pressure is reduced.
Source: González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10.59387/LFPR6347 .
Text in the chart: hard-coral cover (three times)
With wildfires, not every disturbance is the same. Its intensity matters, as does the condition of the ecosystem beforehand. A forest weakened by drought, pests or poor management may fare worse; a reef burdened by pollution, overfishing or coastal development may be less able to withstand a marine heatwave.But this resilience can be strengthened through effective management and the reduction of local pressures to give corals a greater chance of survival and recovery. Effective management cannot stop the ocean from warming, but it can influence how reefs respond.
Regionally, coral-reef trajectories diverge, shaped by distinct pressures and environmental conditions. Four of the ten GCRMN regions exhibited long-term declines, four showed no evidence of net change and two demonstrated increases. This highlights both the urgency of the crisis and the opportunity for policymakers to influence outcomes for coral reefs and the communities that depend upon them.
Source: Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025.₹
González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10. 59387/LFPR6347
Policy treats coral reef pressures separately: warming through the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), biodiversity through the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and fishing and pollution through national governments. But the reef experiences them all simultaneously. The ecological consequences become economic ones: weaker fisheries, declining tourism and less protection for coastal communities.
Reefs safeguard an estimated 5.3m people and $10 9 bn in GDP from storm impacts each decade and between 2000 and 2020 the population within 5km of a reef rose by 46%, underscoring the dependency of communities on the services they provide to humanity. Cutting emissions is essential but insufficient without local management that reduces pressures, and neither works without sustained funding and long-term monitoring.
The next few months will test whether international policy can provide alignment on the necessary actions to safeguard reefs. At the CBD’s COP17 in October, parties will review progress towards the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The draft Global Report on Collective Progress , highlights significant gaps in baselines against which progress can be assessed including coral cover. The GCRMN helps address persistent gaps in marine-biodiversity monitoring by providing the world's most extensive long-term trends on hard-coral cover and reef condition.
The climate process provides a parallel opportunity. The second Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement begins in 2026, assessing collective progress towards the agreement's goals and informing the next generation of national climate commitments. With the breaching of the 1.5°C threshold now considered increasingly likely, as stated in UNEP’s Limiting Overshoot Report , the message is straightforward: limiting warming remains essential, but it must be accompanied by action that strengthens resilience to the warming already occurring.
The UNFCCC's Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue is the most direct bridge between these agendas. Long-term reef monitoring can support that effort by providing a common evidence base: showing how reefs are changing, where resilience is improving and where further action is needed.
Source: Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025.
González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10. 59387/LFPR6347
The question is no longer whether coral reefs are changing, but whether our policies, investments and conservation efforts can keep pace with the scale and speed of that change. The report provides the knowledge needed to act. Accelerating implementation, scaling finance, strengthening protection and embedding the latest science into decision-making have never been more urgent.
The full report, regional chapters and summary for policymakers are now available on GCRMN .

articles.title_orig: CDC sending a ‘disease detective’ to help stop measles outbreak in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: CDC sending a ‘disease detective’ to help stop measles outbreak in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Feds investigate suspicious letters sent to lawmakers and election officials
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is sending one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help curb the state’s growing measles outbreak , a CDC spokesperson said Thursday. That person, a “disease detective” within the agency’s Epidemic Intelligence Service, is scheduled to arrive later this week.
It’s the CDC’s first in-person assistance to the state after a social media feud in August between Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. The two traded jabs following a press briefing where Shapiro announced that two unvaccinated people had died of measles complications and accused Kennedy of spreading vaccine misinformation.
“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said during the briefing.
Kennedy then suggested that the deaths may have been “fabricated,” and that Shapiro was seeking to profit from them politically.
Since August, six people diagnosed with measles have died in Pennsylvania, according to health officials and county coroners. The CDC has acknowledged two of the deaths on its measles outbreak website, saying the other measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are “under review.”
“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson wrote in an email Thursday, adding that director Dr. Erica Schwartz recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection.”
Pennsylvania is experiencing the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 30 years, with at least 1,222 confirmed cases and 225 hospitalizations, although doctors say the actual number of illnesses is likely much higher. The outbreak’s epicenter remains in Lancaster County, but is spreading across the state.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the CDC aid.
The CDC team has previously sent teams to other states with large clusters of measles illnesses: Kansas, New Mexico, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. Such deployments are usually short -term, about one to three weeks. They’re meant to help mobilize and streamline outbreak containment efforts.
In addition to the deployment, the CDC is releasing nearly $4 million to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: What we know about the criminal investigation into US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
articles.title_zh: What we know about the criminal investigation into US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
articles.content_orig:
US government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation".
The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband.
The Wall Street Journal reported that her mobile phone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time.
Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports.
Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship.
Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams".
US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.
Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he had "no concerns" about her citizenship.
Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000.
According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18.
If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately.
After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker.
Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications.
According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee".
The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship.
Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991.
"[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator."
The BBC has contacted Omar for comment.
The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected.
According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration.
Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is revoked. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process.
This appears to be where the groundwork is being laid in the current investigation into Omar.
Trump has repeatedly suggested Omar should be deported, calling for her to "go back" to Somalia.
At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd.
After her home was searched, Omar wrote on X: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "I will not be silenced."
Trump has said the investigation into her has "nothing to do with me".
The timing of the federal probe has defied justice department precedent of not taking action against officials running for office this close to an election.
The raid happened with the November midterm elections only weeks away, drawing condemnation from some of Omar's Democratic colleagues, who said she had been subject to relentless "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations".

articles.title_orig: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast
articles.title_zh: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast
articles.content_orig:
Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’
Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea ⁠coast, setting them ablaze and raising ⁠fresh security concerns on a ​vital shipping route used by Ukraine.
A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came from Russia . “The drones that caused ⁠the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said.
Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the situation in the Black Sea as serious. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk,” he wrote on X. “Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria . This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”
His statement followed a meeting with Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, and Nato’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, on Thursday, where they agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”, Dan said.
Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
A Nato official said the issue would be discussed at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council next week.
The missing crew were from the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged tanker travelling from Tunisia to Romania. All crew on the Yara J, which was struck just inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday, were safe.
Similar incidents in recent weeks have raised fears that the zone is becoming another front in Russia’s war on Ukraine .
Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether Russia was responsible.
Romania shares a 614km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. The country has experienced frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including a daytime encroachment last November that led Nato to scramble fighter jets .
after newsletter promotion
EU leaders were already concerned about drone strikes on merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations, with 11 crew member from the HS Dignity, a cargo ship sailing under a Guinea-Bissau flag, still missing.
On another ship, the Ukrainian-operated Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.
“The results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians,” Radev said after arriving in Brussels for an EU summit on Thursday.
At least 23 sailors have been reported missing or killed after attacks on commercial shipping near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania in the past 10 days, according to Reuters.
Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on Ukraine’s Black Sea infrastructure, forcing Kyiv to turn to Danube river ports and Black Sea routes off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria to export its grain, sunflower oil and other products.
According to a draft summit declaration, EU leaders will say that attacks against civilian shipping, including “member state-flagged vessels, such as the recent attacks in Bulgaria’s and Romania’s exclusive economic zones in the Black Sea, are unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law”.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave 's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at 1,088 bps — a 33% week-over-week jump and 177% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock was down again Thursday, adding to Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive .
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius was down 5% and Iren sank 8% in Thursday trading.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices shed 4% and 6%, respectively, following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft , Meta , IBM and Caterpillar , Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle 's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 288 basis points, a more than 12% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

Oct. 15 (UPI) -- A British woman celebrated her 99th birthday by going wing walking -- and becoming the oldest person to ever do the stunt.
Helga Duffy said she was inspired to attempt the Guinness World Record for the world's oldest wing walker when she news coverage of previous record-holder Betty Bromage performing the feat at the age of 97.
Duffy's wing walk was originally set to take place on her birthday, Sept. 23, but was delayed to Oct. 16.
A Guinness World Records adjudicator was present at RFC Rendcomb Airfield in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, to confirm Duffy's record and present her with a certificate.
The record attempt raised money for Wiltshire and Bath Air Ambulance.
Bromage offered her congratulations to the new record-holder, but indicated she might retake the title.
"I can't wait until I'm 100 and I can do it again, I'll beat you again," she told the BBC.

articles.title_zh: Zelensky Says Ukraine Will Resume Russian Refinery Strikes, Defying Trump
articles.content_orig:
This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected] .
Understanding the conflict four years on.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine defying U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for an energy cease-fire, calls for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and a new border crossing between China and North Korea .
Despite the White House repeatedly urging Kyiv not to target Moscow’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries on Thursday. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times on Thursday.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine defying U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for an energy cease-fire, calls for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and a new border crossing between China and North Korea .
Despite the White House repeatedly urging Kyiv not to target Moscow’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries on Thursday. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times on Thursday.
U.S. President Donald Trump has faced growing pressure to tackle rising fuel prices inflamed by the wars in Ukraine and Iran ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections. In a bid to bring down energy costs, Trump had urged Zelensky to halt all strikes on Russian oil refineries, and on Friday, he suspended U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Then, on Sunday, Trump unilaterally declared an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine while also calling for Zelensky’s removal. Ukraine agreed to the truce and suspended such strikes for three days. However, during those three days, Russian forces launched dozens of ballistic missiles at critical Ukrainian energy infrastructure, plunging around 600,000 people in Kyiv into darkness on Wednesday.
According to Zelensky, the decision to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries was made in response to several controversial decisions out of Washington. They include U.S. military officials reportedly threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues to hit Russian energy targets, new restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink access (which SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused the Trump administration of orchestrating), the White House’s apparent eagerness to ink business deals with Moscow, and Trump’s repeated admiration of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Putin is an enemy for us, and he’s the real evil of today. Absolutely,” Zelensky told the Financial Times . “How can Trump be friends with him?”
Some experts suggest that by bucking Trump’s demands, Zelensky risks widening the rift between them. Trump has long had a rocky relationship with Zelensky, going so far as to berate him during a White House summit in February 2025 and repeatedly parroting Kremlin talking points that question the Ukrainian president’s legitimacy.
Despite the risks, many of Ukraine’s European allies have backed Zelensky’s decision. “The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens, the better, because Russia is funding the war with that,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
Rama stands firm. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama defied calls to step down on Thursday amid sweeping student-led protests demanding his resignation. “My responsibility ‌is to listen, address ‌legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Rama told Reuters . “The alternative would be a betrayal ‌of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership.”
Youth-led demonstrations in Albania, dubbed the Flamingo movement, have accused Rama’s government of widespread corruption, specifically concerning the controversial development of a luxury resort linked to Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. In recent months, protesters have also adopted calls for education reform , citing limited job prospects for recent graduates, high tuition fees, and poor conditions in university building.
As rallies in the capital this week took a violent turn—with protesters attacking government buildings, banks, and businesses—Rama has doubled down on his mandate, insisting that his administration is best poised to bring Albania into the European Union’s fold. “Corruption must be ⁠confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is ​tackling it as ​never before,” Rama said. The EU’s delegation in Tirana, meanwhile, called on demonstrators to “exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence.”
New border crossing. China and North Korea unveiled the largest border crossing between their two countries on Thursday in a sign of ongoing efforts to bolster bilateral trade. The four-lane New Yalu River Bridge spans nearly 2 miles and connects the Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju. Its opening comes barely a month after Pyongyang opened a similar but smaller pass across the Tumen River into Russia.
Construction of the New Yalu River Bridge was delayed for more than a decade. However, the project was accelerated after North Korea opened the bridge to Russia. Analysts believe that the move may have made Chinese officials uneasy as North Korean leader Kim Jong Un draws closer to Moscow; China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner.
Pyongyang, though, remains dedicated to countering international sanctions by fostering closer trade ties with both Beijing and Moscow. Experts believe that the bridges into China and Russia could be used to deliver fuel imports into North Korea as well as circumvent prohibitions on North Korean coal and labor exports.
More time off. Brazil’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment on Wednesday that will shorten the workweek from 44 hours to a maximum of 40 hours. Affecting some 37 million workers, the legislation is the country’s biggest labor rights overhaul in decades, and it delivers a major political win to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva less than two weeks before he faces far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff .
“Those who build Brazil every day also deserve time to live,” Lula wrote on X on Thursday.
Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro , had initially opposed the legislation, arguing that it was designed to improve Lula’s presidential bid; however, he ultimately reversed course after it became clear that public opinion overwhelmingly favored the bill. Only one senator rejected the legislation: former Vice President Hamilton Mourão, who served under the older Bolsonaro.
Lula is expected to sign the legislation into law next week, giving businesses 14 months to comply with the new mandate. Among Lula’s other recent reforms , he has announced new fuel tax cuts, extended existing subsidies designed to lower energy costs, vowed to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses, and boosted welfare payments for university students.
From Charles Dickens to Madonna to King Edward VII, London’s oldest restaurant has long catered to a diverse clientele. This week, the building’s owner, J-P Mayhew, made the decision to ensure that tradition carries on long into the future. Mayhew donated 34-35 Maiden Lane in Covent Garden to the United Kingdom’s National Trust on Wednesday in an effort to safeguard “its bricks and mortar, its famous interior, and its invisible atmosphere.” Along with the building itself, which hosts the historic Rules restaurant , established in 1798, the donation also includes menus, visitor books, photographs, and other memorabilia.

articles.title_orig: Time’s up for ‘leap second’ thanks to Earth’s accelerating spin
articles.title_zh: Time’s up for ‘leap second’ thanks to Earth’s accelerating spin
articles.content_orig:
International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
A fter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.
Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.
The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.
“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”
The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.
“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.
The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.
Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.
Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.
Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.
The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.
“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.
after newsletter promotion
“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.
Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.
To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.
Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.
The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.
Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

articles.title_orig: Alzheimer's Drug ARIA Monitoring: Real-World Study Results
articles.title_zh: Alzheimer's Drug ARIA Monitoring: Real-World Study Results
articles.content_orig:
— Collaboration between prescribers and radiologists is key, lecanemab data show
October 15, 2026 • 3 min read
Rates of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in Alzheimer's disease patients treated with lecanemab (Leqembi) in the real world were consistent with those seen in clinical trials, data from the LEADER study showed.
Anti-amyloid drugs like lecanemab require MRI monitoring for ARIA, making prescriber-radiologist collaboration essential, said Daryl Rhys Jones, PhD, of drugmaker Eisai in Nutley, New Jersey, at the American Society of Functional Neuroradiology meeting in Newport Beach, California.
ARIA is a consequence of amyloid in blood vessel walls. Two types of ARIA can emerge after anti-amyloid drug treatment: ARIA with edema or effusion (ARIA-E) or ARIA with hemosiderin or hemorrhage (ARIA-H).
In the real-world LEADER study, ARIA rates appeared to be lower than rates seen in the phase III CLARITY AD trial of lecanemab, though the differences may not be significant:
The median time to ARIA-E was 3.4 months, Jones reported. Results were similar between 1.5T and 3T MRI. "This suggests that the power of MRI is not really making a difference in detection, at least in the real world," he told MedPage Today.
ARIA rates in LEADER were consistent with other real-world evidence, including data from the ALZ-NET registry , he added.
Lecanemab, an antibody directed against aggregated soluble and insoluble forms of amyloid beta, was approved in 2023 to treat mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease and mild Alzheimer's dementia. The drug carries a boxed warning that ARIA-E or ARIA-H can occur, with a notice that APOE4 homozygotes have a higher incidence of ARIA than heterozygotes and noncarriers.
ARIA is often asymptomatic, and in rare cases, it can be fatal. Lecanemab prescribing information calls for MRI at baseline, then after 1, 2, 3, and 6 months of treatment to monitor for ARIA.
LEADER is an ongoing, multisite, retrospective study that evaluates lecanemab in clinical settings. It incorporates surveys and interviews with healthcare practitioners with chart and electronic medical record data for up to 50 patients per site.
This interim analysis was based on data from 432 patients with early Alzheimer's disease. All participants received at least seven biweekly lecanemab infusions. Some received intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous maintenance treatment after 18 months of IV initiation treatment. Participants had an average of 520.7 days on lecanemab and an average of 25.8 doses.
The LEADER study includes diverse real-world settings, Jones noted. "We didn't just select academic centers that might have extensive experience," he said. "There are general neurologists included in LEADER who were not part of CLARITY AD, so they were treating these patients for the first time. Yet, they were able to implement lecanemab and successfully monitor for the safety of lecanemab in their patients."
Close prescriber-radiologist collaboration was key to that success, Jones observed. This meant establishing communication between neurologists and radiologists  --  "not just themselves, but their front staff, who might be involved with scheduling, and the administrative team at the site," he said.
"It is very important ... to ensure that the radiologist understood what was needed, because the neurologist needs to know, OK, there is no ARIA, I can continue with treatment, or OK, there is ARIA, but this is asymptomatic and mild," Jones pointed out. There needs to be "very clear guidance to the neuroradiologist about what they should be describing for the neurologist," he said.
The analysis included 12 LEADER sites, "but we've expanded now to 20 sites and we're expanding our patient numbers as well," Jones noted. "And, importantly, we're now looking at subcutaneous administration," he added, which the FDA approved earlier this year.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for our free weekly newsletter to get the latest.
Update, Oct. 15, 3:45 p.m.: This story has been updated to reflect that a suspicious letter was sent to Pennsylvania.
Update, Oct. 15, 3 p.m.: This story has been updated to reflect that a suspicious letter was sent to Connecticut.
Correction, Oct. 15: This story has been corrected with the fact that the FBI disclosed its investigation on Thursday, not Friday.
The FBI said Thursday that it is investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to election officials across the nation, an unusually widespread example of election workers being physically threatened during a highly charged midterm campaign.
Federal officials have been speaking with targeted leaders across the country as they work to get a handle on the scope of the apparent attack. Three election officials briefed on the evolving investigation said they were told more than 100 letters were sent to people and groups across the country. The list includes at least one U.S. senator and a polling organization.
Officials in Louisiana and Oklahoma said they received suspicious letters containing a powdery white substance. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose and New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan said that federal officials had intercepted similar letters bound for their offices, and the Pennsylvania Department of State said the U.S. Postal Service blocked delivery of a suspicious letter on Wednesday. The FBI also informed the Connecticut secretary of state a letter had been intercepted. The local FBI field office confirmed it had “received multiple interceptions.”

“Election officials should never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties, and there is no place in a peaceful democracy for violence, threats or acts of intimidation,” LaRose said. “We have a duty to the citizens of Ohio to deliver secure and accessible elections, and these kinds of cowardly threats will not deter us from that mission.”
The FBI said it could not confirm specific cases, but did say its investigation is expansive.
“The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices,” the FBI said. “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident.”
Attacks on elected officials have been on the rise in recent years. In 2024, suspicious packages were sent to election officials in at least six states.

articles.title_orig: School roof collapse in Pakistan kills at least 35 and injures more than 50
articles.title_zh: School roof collapse in Pakistan kills at least 35 and injures more than 50
articles.content_orig:
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.
Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.
The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.
Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.
Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.
"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."
"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."
Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".
The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.
Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.
There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.
The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.
Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.
The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away.
The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary".
"We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said.
Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency.
In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed.
And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers .

articles.title_orig: ANALYSIS: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia as China suspected of assisting
articles.title_zh: ANALYSIS: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia as China suspected of assisting
articles.content_orig:
Middle East expert Behnam Ben Taleblu ties Houthi airport attacks to Iranian threats and warns of possible Russian involvement.
Iran-backed Houthis launched a series of attacks on Saudi Arabian airports through Sunday, reportedly killing at least 14 people, including an American, and injuring more than 300 others, according to reports .
The attacks heightened fears of a wider Middle East war as regional experts warned of "cross-domain escalation" amid heightened tensions over Washington's September actions against Iran's aviation sector.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for earlier attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, while U.S. officials blamed the Iran-backed group for Saturday's strike, which reportedly killed 13 people and injured more than 300.
SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid International Airport after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said another attack on Sunday killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others. Meanwhile, an airport in Dammam, in the kingdom's Eastern Province, was also reportedly targeted by the Houthis.
"Cross-domain escalation by Iran and its proxies will continue to be a primary strategy," Behnam Ben Taleblu , senior director of the Iran Program and a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Sunday.
"The emphasis on aviation targets connects directly to the closing of Iran's aviation sector and sanctions imposed on its commercial airlines under the U.S. maximum pressure campaign," he warned.
RUBIO ACCUSES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES
Smoke was reported near King Khalid International Airport, seen above, as regional tensions and Houthi attacks heightened security concerns in Saudi Arabia. (AFP via Getty Images)
The Houthis also renewed warnings Sunday, urging airlines, airport workers and travelers to avoid Saudi airports as Saudi Arabia vowed to retaliate for the deadly attacks.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned Saturday's attack, confirming that an American was among those killed and calling for an immediate end to the violence.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, left open the possibility of U.S. involvement in Saudi Arabia's military campaign against the Houthis, saying, "We may. We're gonna look at it. We move very quickly."
The escalation comes nearly three weeks after a senior Iranian official threatened to paralyze neighboring countries' airports if they cooperated with U.S. efforts to restrict Iranian flights.
THE HOUTHIS AREN'T SOMEBODY ELSE'S PROBLEM. AMERICA CAN'T AFFORD TO LOOK AWAY
Mohsen Rezaei was named secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. A former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps general and member of the Expediency Discernment Council, as well as the secretary of the Supreme Council for Economic Coordination and the Iranian government's Economic Committee, attends a ceremony at Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's shrine in southern Tehran, Iran, on June 4, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto)
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned Sept. 23 that Iran would prevent neighboring countries' airports from operating if they cooperated with Washington's efforts to restrict Iranian flights, according to Reuters .
"This rapid targeting reflects earlier threats made by Iranian officials, including a veiled threat from the Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warning that U.S. sanctions on Iran's aviation sector would lead to retaliatory threats against neighboring aviation infrastructure," Taleblu said.
Iran has long supported the Houthis, but the extent of Tehran's involvement in the latest airport attacks has not been independently established.
The escalation has also renewed scrutiny of reports that Russia has provided intelligence and technical assistance to the Houthis.
FOILED TERROR PLOT AT BOMBER BASE SIGNALS WIDER THREAT TO US MILITARY INSTALLATIONS: EXPERT
Yemen's Houthi armed forces patrol as Yemeni prisoners loyal to the Houthis arrive in the capital of Sanaa on Sept. 12, 2026, after being released on the west coast where they had been held by Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces. (AFP via Getty Images)
At a Sept. 1 House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing , lawmakers pressed experts on allegations that Russia is providing intelligence and technical support to the Houthis.
"Beyond offering diplomatic cover, there are persistent reports of Russian satellite collaboration, advisory support, and intelligence targeting assistance, as well as unproven allegations regarding select anti-ship systems."
HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS
Yemen's Iran-backed armed Houthi group has warned they will move to shutter the Bab Al-Mandeb Strait through missile-drone attacks if Gulf nations join the US-Israel war on Iran. (Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images)
But he also linked the latest attacks to a broader military escalation as the Houthis expand their territorial control in Yemen.
"This surge did not occur in a vacuum," Taleblu said. "Since April, the Houthis have made territorial gains and pushed back against Saudi forces despite a period of diplomatic lull."

"Airport attacks allow Iran and its regional proxies to inflict pain on Arab states, Israel, and remaining U.S. forces," Taleblu said.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: I’ve Tested Echo Shows and Nest Hubs. Here’s How Apple’s HomeView Display Stacks Up
articles.title_zh: I’ve Tested Echo Shows and Nest Hubs. Here’s How Apple’s HomeView Display Stacks Up
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
The HomeView , announced Tuesday and available on Nov. 13, is Apple’s first-ever smart home display and a new way to control smart home devices or interact with Siri AI. But Apple has significant catching-up to do in this space, because its top competitors have been in the game for a while.
I’ve been testing Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays since they first launched in 2017, and started trying out Google Nest Hubs – originally the Google Home Hub – in 2018. Since then, both brands have released multiple smart speaker models, adding and ditching various features. (And sometimes canceling entire lines – anyone remember the Facebook Portal ?)
That means the stylish HomeView has a chance to learn from past smart display mistakes and differentiate itself in buyers’ eyes, including the Echo Show 11 and the 10-inch Google Nest Hub Max I use at home. Now that we have details and I’ve tried out the Apple HomeView in person, I have several thoughts for anyone considering which smart display to buy.
The HomeView looks great. It immediately reminds me of the Echo Show 11, with the screen mounted on a low-set, domed base housing the speakers. With the discontinued Echo Show 10 , Amazon tried an auto-rotating base that followed people as they moved, but it frequently bumped into things, which annoyed me. So I’m glad to see this display is stationary.
At 7 inches, the HomeView is also tiny.
CNET Smart Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar, who tested out the HomeView at a press briefing, reported that others at Apple’s event complained that the screen was too small. Based on my experience with smart displays, I wholeheartedly agree: It’s significantly smaller than any competitor models made for the same spaces. I’m confused as to why Apple added a screen better suited to a bedroom smart clock than to a tabletop display.
Those Liquid Retina details and colors look great, and maybe a screen this size was the only way to keep the price below $300. But it also hampers some of the best uses of a smart display, like making video calls and watching movies. Apple may have demonstrated Pluribus playing on the HomeView, but I can guarantee you won’t want to watch it on a 7-inch screen from halfway across the kitchen. You won’t be able to catch many details of those Siri “Start Cooking” instructions or FaceTimes with the family, either.
There’s a reason both Amazon and Google have been steadily inched up the size of their flagship smart displays. They’re useful as second TVs or video guides and they need the screen real estate to pull it off. I know from experience that screens under 8 inches don’t cut it unless you’re about a foot or two away.
But wait — there are also wall-mounting options. Google Nest falls way behind here, but you can buy the HomeView as a wall mount version, and Amazon offers a few wall-mounted Echo Shows, too. Kumar said the wall-mounted version of the HomeView looks good, but it also requires professional installation to hide the wired power connection, which will drive your bills well beyond $300. While the result looks amazing, the wired plug-in model may be more practical. Keep in mind that the cheapest wall mount Apple sells with the HomeView costs an additional $60.
I’m also worried about the size of the display on a wall mount, too. The Echo Show 21 ($500) offers a 21-inch touchscreen for your home, as well as a built-in Fire TV platform for watching shows. That much screen real estate still feels more useful than a 7-inch display, which seems more like a security system and lighting hub than an all-purpose station.
I’ve pitted the big three voice assistants against each other in the past, and recently tested which can predict the weather best . Gemini for Home is fine, if a little boring, and very accurate. Siri is snappy when controlling Apple Home devices , but falls behind elsewhere. Alexa Plus, however, is my favorite for smart display use.
Alexa Plus is chatty by nature , but also offers several different personalities to choose from, an option other voice assistants don’t have. Amazon’s integration with Echo Shows has numerous benefits, like showing you the previous details of your conversation so you can keep it going more easily, or displaying extra information on request. Alexa AI is overconfident and sometimes insists it can do things it can’t, but this is an issue with many LLM chatbots.
My favorite Alexa Plus ability is integration with third-party apps, an area where other voice assistants haven’t caught up yet. You can use an Echo Show and Alexa Plus to order food from GrubHub or Uber Eats without lifting a finger, or arrange for an Uber ride from across the room. You can also buy tickets on Ticketmaster or make reservations with OpenTable via Alexa, and Amazon continues to add new integrations for me to test.
Alexa Plus now offers compatibility with some very useful apps, both new and returning.
There’s no indication that Siri AI includes such third-party app support on the HomeView. Apple says, “HomeView supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone,” but doesn’t give many details, and I haven’t seen signs that the HomeView/Siri AI combo will support services or bookings like Alexa Plus can.
But Siri’s AI does win on some accounts, carving out capabilities that Alexa Plus and Gemini for Home don’t have. From the examples Apple showed, it looks like Siri can naturally search your email and texting apps to bring up messages, recipes or other info, something the other voice assistants can’t (Gemini only does this on phones, with the right permissions). You can also customize Siri AI in unique ways, like speeding up or slowing down the voice, which I really like for ease of use and accessibility.
I still prefer Alexa Plus overall, with its chatty asides, personalities to play with and connections to useful third-party apps. I’m looking forward to testing Siri AI on the HomeView to see just what it can do and if Apple adds further integrations. Pricing could also work in Siri AI’s favor, depending on what iCloud Plus subscription is needed to enable all features. If you’re not an Amazon Prime member, Alexa Plus costs a steep $20 a month to fully enable, and Gemini for Home is priced similarly, so Apple could step ahead if Siri AI costs are low.
While Kumar explored how the HomeView worked, he noted that he used an Echo Show to control his smart home and said that, “the result is… functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.”
It’s not an uncommon frustration with the Matter standard and home hubs. Linking multiple smart devices to Alexa or Google hubs and using smart displays for control can be challenging. Interfaces are sometimes wonky, and you can’t always find the settings you want. Devices disappear and need to be reconnected or updated to work again. Voice assistants may not recognize commands that previously worked.
Here, Apple’s tightly knit ecosystem and careful management of the Apple Home app offer a distinct advantage. Kumar saw how the HomeView could effortlessly find and pair with compatible devices, which he compared to setting up a new pair of AirPods. Siri AI can also offer personalization based on facial recognition or manual profile creation, with speedy customization options.
As with HomePods, you can also hand off content between iPhones and the display. Other little Apple tricks, like an instant Find My map displayed to locate missing Apple items, are also included. It already feels more seamless than both the past smart display experiences Kumar and I have had, which is enticing.
The only issue is device support, which tends to be more limited for Apple than other platforms. The company has come a long way in addressing this with its new line of security cameras, a smart lock, and a smart thermostat announced at

articles.title_orig: Man shot by ICE in NYC's Marble Hill said federal officers never identified themselves
articles.title_zh: Man shot by ICE in NYC's Marble Hill said federal officers never identified themselves
articles.content_orig:
